The Independent National Electoral Commission has said it will not be able to conduct a comprehensive clean-up of the national voters’ register before the 2027 general elections, citing time constraints and public resistance to its earlier plan to revalidate the register. The commission’s chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, disclosed this while appearing on a Bereke Family TV programme aired on Friday. Amupitan said the commission had initially proposed a six-month exercise to remove deceased persons, underage voters, incomplete registrations and duplicate entries from the register but shelved the plan after opposition. His explanation follows controversy over alleged irregularities in the preliminary voter register, particularly duplicate entries that drew criticism on social media. Speaking during the programme, Amupitan said the commission had decided to postpone the comprehensive exercise until after the 2027 elections, although it was addressing cases of multiple registrations following public complaints. He said: “The complaint that came out on social media, those ones, majorly when we investigated further, we discovered it was the old register, the new one we have dealt with it. But the one that everybody is shouting about, complaining about duplication were mostly from the old register. “In February, we decided that the foundation of a good election is a valid voters’ register. Let us do the validation because people who have already died were still in the register, and many names were doubled. “We said the process would only take six months. Let us clean up so that people can come and update their details, but Nigerians said no. So, we said we would do it after the election.” Edo voter register hits 2.8 million Stay at polling units to protect votes, Obi urges voters PHOTOS: Obi’s supporters gather in Onitsha for town hall rally Amupitan said the commission had planned to use improved technology to detect irregularities that earlier registration systems missed. He added that the proposed exercise was also meant to address incomplete registrations and underage entries, besides removing deceased persons. Amupitan, however, said the commission could no longer carry out the entire exercise before the next general elections because of limited time. He said INEC had instead returned to tackling duplicate entries, especially those flagged by the public. Amupitan said some cases were particularly disturbing, with the same person appearing in the register with as many as five different photographs. He said: “We cannot do everything now; we have no time to do it, but we can do duplications, those ones they are flagging. “Some of the cases involve five pictures of the same person. It is very ridiculous, truly, and we cannot close our eyes to it. We are doing that right now to ensure that the register is clean.” Amupitan also disclosed that the review had reduced the number of registered voters, adding that the commission would release the final register once the ongoing review ended. He said INEC had initially scheduled December 15 for releasing the final register but was reviewing the timeline after widespread complaints. Olufemi Adediran
